pages.name: Two letters
pages.text: Three windings meet at the star point. Each winding of this 440 V supply gives 254 V. The motor's frame is bonded to the hull. Two letters name what the star point is tied to. The first is the star point: T for earth, from the French terre, or I for isolated. The second is how the frames reach earth. N, for neutral, means a conductor back to the star point. T means an electrode of their own.

pages.name: Reading IT
pages.task: A supply is marked IT. What do its two letters tell you? The drawing shows TN for now.
pages.answer: The star point is isolated from earth. The frames go to earth.
pages.why: Read the letters in order. The first is the star point: I, isolated. The second is the frames: T, to earth. On a ship that earth is the hull.

pages.name: TN: the loop closes
pages.text: On TN the fault current runs out of L1 and into the frame. It comes back along the protective conductor to the star point and up L1's winding. Say that metal loop is 0.5 Ω, so 254 ÷ 0.5 = 508 A. The breaker trips at once.

pages.name: Why TN trips
pages.task: Why does the breaker trip on TN?
pages.answer: The protective conductor gives the current a low-resistance way back to the star point.
pages.why: Current only flows round a complete loop. The protective conductor closes it back to the star point through metal. That loop is a fraction of an ohm. So 254 V drives hundreds of amps, and the breaker trips at once.

pages.name: A TT fault
pages.task: A TT supply has electrodes of 20 Ω and 200 Ω, the same 254 V winding, a 32 A breaker and a 30 mA RCD. About what current flows at a fault to frame, and what trips?
pages.answer: About 1.2 A, and the RCD trips
pages.why: The loop is 20 + 200 = 220 Ω, so 254 ÷ 220 = 1.15 A, about 1.2 A. A breaker needs many times its rating to trip at once. An RCD trips on 30 mA that does not come back.

pages.name: A floating star point
pages.task: Same motor, same fault on L1, but the star point is floating. What happens?
pages.answer: A few milliamps flow, the motor runs on and an alarm lights.
pages.why: The fault reaches the hull, but the star point is not tied to it. The only loop runs through 100 kΩ of insulation, so 254 V drives about 2.5 mA. That trips nothing.

pages.name: Why insulate?
pages.task: Why would a ship's supply be insulated?
pages.answer: So an earth fault does not take out an essential service at once
pages.why: An insulated supply runs on through its first earth fault. So the steering, the pumps and the lights stay on while the fault is found.

pages.name: Which system?
pages.task: A supply's first earth fault draws about 2 A, and an RCD trips. What is its star point tied to? The drawing shows TN for now.
pages.answer: Earth, through its own electrode: TT
pages.why: A trip means the star point is tied to earth. A few amps, not hundreds, means the loop runs through the ground between two electrodes. That is TT.

pages.name: TN-S
pages.task: A board's drawing says TN-S. The S means its protective conductor is separate from the neutral. What happens at its first earth fault to a frame?
pages.answer: A large current flows and the breaker trips
pages.why: T first: the star point is tied to earth. N second: the frames go back to it through a protective conductor. In TN-S that conductor is separate from the neutral. So the loop is all metal, and the breaker trips.
